answer:
FINAL HYPOTHESIS (data-grounded):

"The 'advantage' of Black students (their Black-minus-non-Black differential) in college-degree-level attainment is inversely related to family socioeconomic status. In the NLSY79 1979 snapshot (12,098 complete cases), Black students from low-parental-SES families complete ≥14 years of schooling at essentially the same rate as non-Black students (2.4% vs 2.7%), and at ≥13 years even slightly exceed them (5.7% vs 4.4%); but as parental SES rises the Black rate falls further and further behind the non-Black rate — at the highest SES level Black students attain ≥14 years at only about half the non-Black rate (7.3% vs 13.6%, a ≈5–7 percentage-point deficit; 16.4% vs 24.2% at ≥13). The Black advantage therefore declines monotonically across Low→Mid→High SES levels, from roughly parity/slightly positive to a large disadvantage at the top. This pattern replicates at the ≥13, ≥14, and ≥15 schooling thresholds and in the age≥19 subsample (confirming it is not an artifact of the 1979 age censoring), but it is sensitive to how SES is measured: with family income as SES the gap is instead largest at low income and narrows with income (significant opposite-signed interaction), and with 1996 family wealth the gap is small and flat — so the conclusion holds under the exogenous background-SES (parental education) definition. Literal BA completion (grade ≥16) is too rare (0.3%, 39 cases) in this single-wave, age-censored snapshot to be analyzed directly, so ≥14 years of completed schooling is used as the college-degree-level attainment proxy with ≥13/≥15/≥16 all reported."

[Interpretation for the posed question: the Black advantage in (proxy) BA-degree-level completion is NEGATIVELY related to SES — it is strongest at low SES and disappears/reverses into a deficit at high SES.]

KEY TABLES (outcome rates %, parental-education SES terciles, complete case n=12,098):
GC14 (≥14 yrs):
  Low:  BLACK 2.41 | HISP 2.53 | NBNH 2.69   → Black−NBNH adv −0.28pp (pooled nonBlack −0.22)
  Mid:  BLACK 4.53 | HISP 2.89 | NBNH 4.27   → adv +0.26 (+0.63)
  High: BLACK 7.26 | HISP 7.60 | NBNH 13.58  → adv −6.32 (−4.99)
GC13 (≥13): adv NBNH pp = +1.21 / +0.15 / −7.82
GC15 (≥15): adv NBNH pp = −0.25 / −0.69 / −2.76
BA16 (≥16): ≈0 everywhere (n=2,0,3 Black by level; unusable)
n per cell (BLACK/HISP/NBNH): Low 1204/1106/1712; Mid 309/1005/2717; High 372/816/2857.

STATISTICS (age- and sex-controlled logits, parental-ed SES):
- Linear black×SES trend (0/1/2): GC13 coef −0.243 (p=0.036, significant); GC14 coef −0.260 (p=0.106, marginal); GC15 −0.188 (p=0.471); BA16 −0.065 (p=0.912).
- Low-vs-High contrast: GC13 −0.376 (p=0.111), GC14 −0.370 (p=0.260).
- Age≥19 subsample (n=5,227): GC14 adv NBNH pp = +0.22 / +3.22 / −7.89; GC13 = +4.84 / +5.14 / −6.04 (pattern strengthens; interaction GC13 p=0.086).
- Sensitivity — GC14 by other SES: income-79 adv NBNH pp = −9.44 / −1.39 / −0.67 (opposite pattern, interaction +0.905, p=0.017); wealth-96 adv NBNH pp = −0.72 / −1.14 / +0.23 (flat, n=6,954).
- Imputation robustness (race-mean par_ed, n=445 filled): GC14 adv NBNH −0.26 / +0.69 / −6.51 vs complete-case −0.28 / +0.26 / −6.32 — stable.

WORKFLOW: (1) cleaned 'Highest grade completed, 1979' (dropped invalid code 95, n=2; missing n=152); derived four attainment thresholds (≥13/≥14/≥15 literal BA≥16). (2) Built SES measures — parent-education composite (mean of mother's & father's grade, one-parent fallback), family income 1979, family net wealth 1996 — each split into population terciles (Low/Mid/High). (3) Complete-case analytic sample (n=12,098) for primary; per-cell N reported. (4) Computed race by SES-level attainment rates and Black-minus-pooled-nonBlack and Black-minus-NBNH advantages (pp). (5) Age- and sex-controlled logistic regressions testing Black×SES interactions (Low-vs-High contrast; linear trend). (6) Sensitivity: age≥19 de-censoring subsample; alternative SES measures; parental-ed imputation. All executed in analysis_main.py; summary saved to results_summary.csv.

payload.hypothesis: The Black advantage (Black-minus-non-Black differential) in college-degree-level attainment is negatively related to family socioeconomic status: it is near zero at low parental SES (>=14yrs: 2.4% vs 2.7%; >=13yrs: 5.7% vs 4.4% - slightly positive) and declines monotonically to a large deficit at high parental SES (>=14yrs: 7.3% vs 13.6%, about 5-7pp; >=13yrs: 16.4% vs 24.2%, about 8pp). The pattern holds across >=13/>=14/>=15 thresholds and the age>=19 subsample (not an age-censoring artifact), but reverses/flattens under income- or wealth-based SES, so it is specific to exogenous background (parental-education) SES. Literal BA (grade>=16) is too sparse (0.3%) to analyze in this single 1979 snapshot.
payload.workflow: Cleaned Highest grade completed 1979 (dropped invalid grade 95, n=2; missing n=152) into thresholds >=13/>=14/>=15/>=16. Built SES measures (parental-education composite with one-parent fallback; family income 1979; family net wealth 1996) as population terciles Low/Mid/High. Computed race-by-SES attainment rates plus Black-minus-pooled-nonBlack and Black-minus-NBNH advantages (pp). Fitted age-and-sex-controlled logistic regressions testing Black x SES interactions (Low-vs-High contrast and 0/1/2 linear trend). Sensitivities: age>=19 subsample (de-censoring), alternative SES measures (income79, wealth96), and parental-ed mean-imputation. All in analysis_main.py; results_summary.csv saved.
